title: Single-Variable Calculus
description: Limits, derivatives, integrals, series and Taylor approximation: the calculus that every machine learning derivation uses.
overview: Calculus is the mathematics of change and accumulation. In machine learning the derivative says how a loss changes when a parameter moves, and so tells us which way to step. The integral accumulates probability over a range, and defines expectations of continuous quantities. Series and Taylor approximations replace complicated functions by simple ones near a point, which is the idea behind gradient descent and Newton's method.

This chapter is a compact review of one-variable calculus, selecting the parts that machine learning uses and illustrating each with a machine learning function: the sigmoid, the logarithm of a likelihood, the Gaussian integral and the geometric series of discounted rewards.
objectives: Compute derivatives using the sum, product, quotient and chain rules, and differentiate the exponential, logarithm and sigmoid.
Find and classify the minima of a function with the first and second derivative tests.
Evaluate definite integrals with the fundamental theorem, substitution and integration by parts, including the Gaussian integral.
Sum geometric series and write Taylor series with an error estimate.
Use the standard inequalities 1 + x ≤ e^x and ln x ≤ x − 1, and the log-sum-exp identity.

sections.title: Functions, limits and continuity
body: A function f assigns to each input x one output f(x). The **limit** lim_{x→a} f(x) = L means that f(x) can be made as close to L as we like by taking x close enough to a (but not equal to it). A function is **continuous** at a if the limit exists and equals f(a): the graph has no jump at a. Polynomials, exponentials, logarithms (for x > 0) and the sigmoid are continuous everywhere on their domains.

Two functions occur constantly. The **exponential** eˣ, with e = 2.71828…, is the function that equals its own derivative and turns addition into multiplication, e^{a+b} = e^a e^b. Its inverse is the **natural logarithm**, ln x, with ln(ab) = ln a + ln b, ln(a/b) = ln a − ln b, and ln(a^p) = p ln a.

body.key: The logarithm turns products into sums. A likelihood is a product of many probabilities, each below 1, which underflows in floating-point arithmetic and has awkward derivatives. Its logarithm is a sum, which is stable, easy to differentiate and has the same maximizer, because ln is increasing.

example.title: Log of a product
example.problem: Ten independent observations each have probability 0.01 under a model. Compute the likelihood and the log-likelihood.
example.solution: The likelihood is 0.01¹⁰ = 10⁻²⁰. The log-likelihood is 10 ln 0.01 = 10(−4.605) = −46.05. A thousand such observations would give 10⁻²⁰⁰⁰, which underflows a 64-bit float (smallest about 10⁻³⁰⁸), while the log-likelihood −4605 is perfectly representable.

body: A useful limit: lim_{n→∞} (1 + x/n)ⁿ = eˣ. It explains continuous compounding, and why the probability that an example is absent from a bootstrap sample of size m, (1 − 1/m)^m, tends to e⁻¹ = 0.368.

sections.title: Derivatives and differentiation rules
body: If you drive 150 km in 2 hours, your average speed is 75 km/h. The speedometer shows something sharper: your speed at one instant. To estimate it, compare your position now with your position a tiny moment later and divide the distance by the time. The smaller the moment, the better the estimate, and the value it settles on is the derivative. For a loss function, the derivative with respect to a weight says how much the loss rises per unit increase of the weight, which tells us which way to move it. The **derivative** of f at x is the instantaneous rate of change, the limit of the slope of secant lines:

body.eq: f′(x) = lim_{h→0} ( f(x + h) − f(x) ) / h

body: Geometrically it is the slope of the **tangent line**. The tangent line at a is y = f(a) + f′(a)(x − a), the best linear approximation to f near a.

body: The **chain rule** is the engine of backpropagation: the derivative of a composition is the product of the derivatives of its links, taken from the outside in. A deep network is a long composition, and its gradient is a long chain-rule product.

example.title: Derivative of the sigmoid and of the log-sigmoid
example.problem: Find σ′(x) for σ(x) = 1/(1 + e^{−x}), and the derivative of ln σ(x).
solution: Write σ = (1 + e^{−x})⁻¹. By the chain rule, σ′ = −(1 + e^{−x})⁻² · (−e^{−x}) = e^{−x}/(1 + e^{−x})².
For the log: (ln σ)′ = σ′/σ = 1 − σ(x). This is why the gradient of the logistic regression log-likelihood is simply (y − h)x.

example.title: A squared-error loss
example.problem: Differentiate L(w) = ½(wx − y)² with respect to w.
example.solution: Let u = wx − y, so L = ½u². Then dL/dw = u · du/dw = (wx − y) x. The error times the input, as in the LMS rule.

sections.title: Optimization with derivatives
body: To minimize f, look for **critical points**, where f′(x) = 0 (the tangent is flat). Then use the second derivative, which measures curvature:

list: f″(x) > 0 at a critical point: a local minimum (the graph curves up).
f″(x) = 0: inconclusive. A function with f″ ≥ 0 everywhere is **convex**, and every critical point is then a global minimum; this is why least squares and logistic regression are easy to optimize.

example.title: Minimizing a quadratic
example.solution: f′(x) = 2x − 4 = 0 gives x = 2. f″ = 2 > 0, so it is a minimum with f(2) = 1. The same procedure finds the sample mean as the minimizer of Σ(x_i − μ)²: setting −2Σ(x_i − μ) = 0 gives μ = mean.

body.h: Gradient descent and Newton's method in one variable

body: **Gradient descent** moves against the derivative: x ← x − α f′(x). For a quadratic f = ½cx² the update is x ← (1 − αc)x, so it converges if |1 − αc| < 1, i.e. α < 2/c. A larger curvature requires a smaller step.
**Newton's method** for solving g(x) = 0 replaces g by its tangent line and jumps to where that line crosses zero:
Applied to g = f′ it finds critical points: x ← x − f′(x)/f″(x), which scales the step by the inverse curvature.

example.title: Newton's method for √2
example.problem: Solve g(x) = x² − 2 = 0 starting at x₀ = 1.
example.solution: g′ = 2x. x₁ = 1 − (−1)/2 = 1.5. x₂ = 1.5 − 0.25/3 = 1.41667. x₃ = 1.41667 − 0.006944/2.8333 = 1.414216. The true value is 1.414214: the number of correct digits roughly doubles each step (quadratic convergence).

sections.title: Integrals
body: The integral is accumulation. If f(t) is the speed of a car at time t, the distance traveled is the sum of speed × tiny time step over all the steps, and that sum is the area under the speed curve. If f is a probability density, the area under it between a and b is the probability that the value lands in that range. The derivative and the integral undo each other, which is the content of the fundamental theorem below. The **definite integral** ∫_a^b f(x) dx is the signed area under the graph of f between a and b, the limit of **Riemann sums** Σ f(x_i)Δx. The **fundamental theorem of calculus** links it to derivatives: if F′ = f (F is an **antiderivative**), then

list: **Substitution** undoes the chain rule: with u = g(x), ∫ f(g(x)) g′(x) dx = ∫ f(u) du.
**Integration by parts** undoes the product rule: ∫ u dv = uv − ∫ v du.

example.title: An exponential distribution
example.problem: Show that p(x) = λe^{−λx} for x ≥ 0 integrates to 1, and compute its mean ∫₀^∞ x λe^{−λx} dx.
solution: For the mean use integration by parts with u = x and dv = λe^{−λx} dx (so v = −e^{−λx}): ∫₀^∞ x λe^{−λx} dx = [−x e^{−λx}]₀^∞ + ∫₀^∞ e^{−λx} dx = 0 + 1/λ. The mean is 1/λ.

body: The function e^{−x²/2} has no elementary antiderivative, but its integral over the whole line is known exactly:

This is why the normal density has the constant 1/√(2π): N(x; μ, σ²) = (1/(σ√(2π))) exp(−(x − μ)²/(2σ²)). By the substitution u = (x − μ)/σ, the integral over x of the unnormalized exponential is σ√(2π) for any mean and variance. The standard derivation squares the integral and switches to polar coordinates (see Multivariable Calculus).

An integral over an infinite range is an **improper integral**, defined as a limit of integrals over [a, b] as b → ∞. It converges when the integrand decays fast enough: ∫₁^∞ x⁻² dx = 1 converges, while ∫₁^∞ x⁻¹ dx diverges.

sections.title: Series and Taylor approximation
body: A **geometric series** has a constant ratio r between terms. Its partial sum and its limit for |r| < 1 are

This is the formula behind the discounted return of reinforcement learning: a reward of 1 per step with discount γ = 0.9 is worth 1/(1 − 0.9) = 10. It also gives the sum of the learning rate schedules and the error decay of iterative algorithms, which shrinks like r^k.

Zoom in far enough on any smooth curve and it looks like a straight line. Zoom in a little less and it looks like a gentle parabola. The Taylor series makes this precise: near a point, a complicated function can be replaced by a polynomial that matches its value, its slope, its curvature and so on at that point, and each extra term makes the replacement good over a wider range. A smooth function near a point a is approximated by a polynomial whose derivatives match those of f at a:

Truncating after the term of order n leaves an error of size about |x − a|^{n+1} times the next derivative. The first-order truncation is the tangent line, and the second-order one adds curvature. Gradient descent uses the first-order model (and picks a step in which it can be trusted), and Newton's method uses the second-order model.

example.title: Approximating e^{0.1}
example.problem: Estimate e^{0.1} with the Taylor polynomial of order 3 and bound the error.
example.solution: 1 + 0.1 + 0.01/2 + 0.001/6 = 1 + 0.1 + 0.005 + 0.000167 = 1.105167. The true value is 1.105171, so the error is 4 × 10⁻⁶, about the size of the next term 0.1⁴/24 = 4.2 × 10⁻⁶.

example.title: Linearizing the log loss
example.solution: Using ln(1 + x) = x − x²/2 + … with x = −p: −ln(1 − p) = p + p²/2 + p³/3 + …. So for a small error probability p, the log loss of the true class is about p.

sections.title: Convexity and useful inequalities
terms: convex function and its tangent line
body: A function is **convex** if its graph lies below every chord, equivalently if it lies above every tangent line, equivalently (for twice-differentiable functions) f″ ≥ 0. Two consequences are used everywhere.

list: **Tangent bounds.** Since eˣ is convex and its tangent at 0 is 1 + x, we have 1 + x ≤ eˣ for all x. Taking logarithms, ln y ≤ y − 1 for y > 0. These are used to bound probabilities (for example (1 − ε)^m ≤ e^{−εm}, as in the learning theory chapter) and to prove that KL divergence is non-negative.
**Jensen's inequality.** For convex f, f(E[X]) ≤ E[f(X)]; for concave f (such as ln), the inequality reverses: ln E[X] ≥ E[ln X]. It is the key to the EM algorithm.

example.title: Checking the bounds
example.problem: Verify 1 + x ≤ e^x at x = 0.5 and x = −1, and (1 − 0.1)^20 ≤ e^{−2}.

body: Softmax and log-likelihoods of mixtures need ln Σ_i e^{z_i}. If any z_i is large, e^{z_i} overflows (e⁸⁰⁰ is infinity in double precision). Subtract the maximum m = max z_i:

body.eq: ln Σ_i e^{z_i} = m + ln Σ_i e^{z_i − m}

body: Now every exponent is ≤ 0, so nothing overflows, and the largest term equals 1, so the sum cannot underflow to 0.

example.title: Stable log-sum-exp
example.solution: With m = 1001: 1001 + ln(e^{−1} + 1) = 1001 + ln(1.3679) = 1001.3133. Computing e^{1000} directly would overflow.

quiz.q: A bootstrap sample draws m items with replacement from m. For large m, the chance that a particular item is never drawn is about
quiz.why: The chance of missing it on every draw is (1 − 1/m)^m, which tends to e⁻¹ = 0.368. The value 0.632 is the chance it is drawn at least once.

quiz.q: Which statement about replacing a likelihood by its logarithm is FALSE?
quiz.a: It moves the maximizing parameter, because the log compresses large likelihood values
wrong: It turns a product over observations into a sum
It avoids floating-point underflow for many observations
It keeps the same maximizing parameter, since ln is increasing
quiz.why: ln is strictly increasing, so the location of the maximum is unchanged; only the scale of the values changes.

quiz.q: Let f(x) = (x² − 1)/(x − 1) for x ≠ 1, with f(1) undefined. Which statement is correct?
quiz.a: The limit at x = 1 is 2, but f is not continuous there
wrong: The limit at x = 1 does not exist, because f(1) is undefined
The limit at x = 1 is 0, because the numerator vanishes
The limit at x = 1 is 2, so f is continuous there
quiz.why: For x ≠ 1, f(x) = x + 1, so the limit is 2. A limit ignores the value at the point itself; continuity needs the limit to equal f(1), which does not exist.

quiz.q: With σ the sigmoid, σ(ln 3) = 3/4. What is σ′(ln 3)?
quiz.why: σ′ = σ(1 − σ) = 0.75 × 0.25 = 0.1875. The value 0.25 is the maximum of σ′, reached only at x = 0.

quiz.q: What is the derivative of x/(1 + x) for x > −1?
quiz.why: Quotient rule: [1·(1 + x) − x·1]/(1 + x)² = 1/(1 + x)². Adding the two terms in the numerator instead of subtracting gives the last option.

quiz.q: A classifier outputs h = σ(z) = 0.9 for an example whose true label is 1. What is the derivative of ln h with respect to z?
quiz.why: (ln σ)′ = σ′/σ = 1 − σ = 0.1. The value 0.09 is σ′ itself, which omits the division by σ.

quiz.q: Let f(x) = x⁴. At the critical point x = 0 we have f″(0) = 0. What does the second derivative test conclude?
quiz.a: Nothing; the test is inconclusive, though x = 0 is in fact a minimum
wrong: x = 0 is not a critical point
quiz.why: When f″ = 0 the test gives no verdict. Here f(x) ≥ 0 = f(0), so it is a minimum, but this must be shown by other means.

quiz.q: Gradient descent is run on f(x) = 3x² with step size α. For which α does it converge to the minimum?
quiz.why: Here f = ½cx² with c = 6, so the update is x ← (1 − 6α)x, which shrinks when |1 − 6α| < 1, i.e. α < 2/6 = 1/3.

quiz.q: Newton's method minimizes f(x) = eˣ − 2x starting at x₀ = 0. What is x₁?
quiz.why: f′(0) = e⁰ − 2 = −1 and f″(0) = 1, so x₁ = 0 − (−1)/1 = 1. Forgetting the minus sign in the update gives −1.

quiz.q: Newton's method for minimizing f takes the step −f′(x)/f″(x). What does dividing by f″ accomplish?
quiz.a: It makes the step larger where the function is flat and smaller where it is sharply curved
wrong: It makes the step always shorter than a gradient step
It guarantees the step goes uphill in f
It removes the need to evaluate f′
quiz.why: Dividing by the curvature rescales the step to the local quadratic model. It does not shrink every step, and it still needs f′.

quiz.q: What is ∫₀^1 2x e^{x²} dx?
quiz.why: Substitute u = x², du = 2x dx: ∫₀^1 e^u du = e − 1. Forgetting to adjust the limits or the factor 2 gives the other options.

quiz.q: Which improper integral converges?
quiz.why: ∫₁^∞ x^{−3/2} dx = [−2x^{−1/2}]₁^∞ = 2. The integrand must decay faster than 1/x; the other three antiderivatives (ln x, 2√x, x) grow without bound.
Matching exp(−(x − μ)²/(2σ²)) gives 2σ² = 8, so σ = 2, and the integral is σ√(2π). The mean 3 only shifts the curve.

quiz.q: What is Σ_{k=1}^{∞} 0.9^k (the sum starts at k = 1)?
quiz.why: The full sum from k = 0 is 1/(1 − 0.9) = 10; removing the k = 0 term (which equals 1) leaves 9. The formula 1/(1 − r) assumes the sum starts at k = 0.

quiz.q: Using the Taylor series σ(x) ≈ 1/2 + x/4 near 0, what is the estimate of σ(0.2)?
quiz.why: 0.5 + 0.2/4 = 0.55 (the true value is 0.5498). Using a slope of 1/2 gives 0.6, and a slope of 1 gives 0.7.

quiz.q: A second-order Taylor polynomial about a has error of order |x − a|³. If the distance |x − a| is halved, the error shrinks by about a factor of
quiz.why: The error scales as |x − a|³, and (1/2)³ = 1/8. A factor of 4 would correspond to the squared term, the first one that was kept.

quiz.q: X equals 1 or 9 with probability 1/2 each. Which comparison is right?
quiz.a: ln E[X] ≈ 1.61 is larger than E[ln X] ≈ 1.10
wrong: E[ln X] ≈ 1.61 is larger than ln E[X] ≈ 1.10
They are equal, because ln is increasing
They are equal, because E[X] = 5 is the midpoint
quiz.why: E[X] = 5 and ln 5 = 1.61, while E[ln X] = (0 + ln 9)/2 = 1.10. For concave ln, Jensen's inequality gives ln E[X] ≥ E[ln X].

quiz.q: What is ln(e^{500} + e^{500} + e^{500}) computed stably?
quiz.why: Subtracting m = 500 gives 500 + ln(1 + 1 + 1). The maximum alone (500) ignores the other two terms, and ln of a sum is not a sum of the exponents.

quiz.q: Using 1 + x ≤ eˣ with x = −ε, which bound holds for (1 − 0.01)^300?
quiz.why: Since 1 − ε ≤ e^{−ε}, raising to the 300th power gives (1 − 0.01)^300 ≤ e^{−3} ≈ 0.050. The inequality points upper, not lower.

summary: The logarithm turns products into sums, so likelihoods are handled through log-likelihoods.
The derivative is the slope of the tangent line. Use the chain rule for compositions: σ′ = σ(1 − σ), and (ln σ)′ = 1 − σ.

Critical points have f′ = 0; f″ > 0 gives a minimum, and convex functions have only global minima. Gradient descent steps x ← x − αf′ and converges for α < 2/c on a quadratic; Newton's method x ← x − f′/f″ converges quadratically near a minimum.
The fundamental theorem gives ∫_a^b f = F(b) − F(a). The Gaussian integral ∫e^{−x²/2}dx = √(2π) fixes the normal density.
Geometric series sum to 1/(1 − r). Taylor polynomials approximate f near a, and the tangent line is the first-order one.
1 + x ≤ e^x, ln y ≤ y − 1 and Jensen's inequality are used constantly. The log-sum-exp trick keeps softmax numerically stable.

problems.q: Differentiate f(x) = x e^{−x} and find its maximum for x ≥ 0.
problems.solution: By the product rule f′ = e^{−x} − x e^{−x} = (1 − x)e^{−x}, which is zero at x = 1. For x < 1 it is positive and for x > 1 negative, so x = 1 is the maximum, with f(1) = e⁻¹ = 0.368.
problems.a: f′ = (1 − x)e^{−x}; the maximum is at x = 1 with value 0.368.

problems.q: Use Newton's method to find √5 starting from x₀ = 2: do two steps.
Evaluate ∫₀^∞ x² e^{−x} dx by parts.
problems.solution: Let u = x², dv = e^{−x}dx: [−x²e^{−x}]₀^∞ + ∫₀^∞ 2x e^{−x} dx = 0 + 2·∫₀^∞ x e^{−x} dx. The last integral equals 1 (by parts again: [−xe^{−x}] + ∫e^{−x} = 1). So the result is 2.

problems.q: A reinforcement learning agent receives reward 3 at every step with discount γ = 0.8. What is the total discounted reward, and what is it if the episode stops after 5 steps?
Compute ln(e^{−500} + e^{−502}) with the log-sum-exp trick.
